title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Session with Ashoka Investment Club on April 22, 2025
summary: Pabrai discusses mental models with Ashoka students: reciprocation (his Cross-pen mailers), the human aversion to cloning (Sam Walton, Microsoft, and his own copying of Buffett's zero-management-fee partnership), and asking 'What is going on here?' He argues Trump tariffs are mostly irrelevant to businesses like DMart and IndiGo, describes low-cost commodity producers and tiny circles of competence as durable edges, retells the Reysas warehouse investment in Turkey now worth a billion dollars, and admits his biggest flaw was selling great businesses like Kotak and Blue Dart at 'fair value' instead of holding winners.

ideas.idea: Mental models give an unfair advantage; jumpstart your latticework by rereading Munger's Psychology of Human Misjudgment every year.
ideas.detail: The talk took Munger four or five decades to accumulate and is the last chapter of Poor Charlie's Almanack, now published cheaply in India; each rereading surfaces things he swears he is reading for the first time.

ideas.idea: The reciprocation tendency is hardwired but uncalibrated: a $30 Cross pen in a physical mailer creates a favorable opinion that can bring in $10 million.
ideas.detail: Hunter-gatherers stored meat in neighbors' bellies via feasts, encoding reciprocation; Pabrai Funds sends prospects a package with a book, pen and hard copies, and only one or two in a hundred return it because of the friction of doing so.

ideas.idea: Lollapalooza effects happen when multiple mental models push in the same direction, so one plus one equals eleven.
ideas.detail: Munger's observation; his own fund launch combined the cloning model, the reciprocation model and 'what is going on here'.

ideas.idea: Humans have an inexplicable aversion to cloning, so intense cloners like Sam Walton and Microsoft do extremely well.
ideas.detail: The Walton family, 55 years after the IPO and 33 years after Sam's death, still owns 46% of Walmart and is America's richest family; Walton copied Sears, Kmart and every merchant he visited. Windows copied Apple, Word copied WordPerfect, Excel copied Lotus, Bing copied Google ('But It's Not Google', per Buffett), while Microsoft's billions in internal research produced nothing.

ideas.idea: He cloned Buffett's 1956-69 partnership fee structure (zero management fee, 6% hurdle, 25% of profits above) because in 30 years nobody else visibly had.
ideas.detail: When he heard of Buffett in 1994-95 he could not find a single fund using the model, an 'offering gap'; it gave him a unique pitch that he only gets rich when investors get rich. Munger later said a few obscure people had copied it.

ideas.idea: Ask 'What is going on here?' whenever something makes you do a double-take, a lesson from playing duplicate bridge with a former world champion.
ideas.detail: His partner Roger, world champion at 23, plays as if opponents' cards are exposed by constantly asking that question; Pabrai applies it to anomalies in markets.

ideas.idea: Ignore what is popular, understand who you are and go all in on your strengths; school makes you a good test taker, which has no relevance in real life.
ideas.detail: Be curious and read widely while going deep in an area of genuine interest; most real problems have no syllabus and many nobody has figured out.

ideas.idea: Cloning trims 50,000 stocks to 50-60 by taking 20 great investors' top holdings; then circle of competence cuts it to five or ten for a deep dive starting with why they bought.
ideas.detail: Most of the time the correct answer to 'is this in my circle of competence?' is no, so about 45 of the 50-60 disappear.

ideas.idea: Trump tariffs are mostly irrelevant; a business's future is driven by micro factors around it and its competitors, not global macro headlines.
ideas.detail: Tariffs do not make DMart or IndiGo useless businesses; play the tariff out in the context of the specific business and it usually does not matter beyond some slowdown in global GDP.

ideas.idea: He agrees with Trump that India's trade is not fair, and lower Indian barriers would sharpen domestic producers and push resources to where India has an edge.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Andhra rice farmers turned to shrimp with no government program and India overtook Thailand as the world's top shrimp exporter; India has edges in pharma and outsourced IT. Farm-size restrictions are a shackle: the US feeds itself with under 2% in farming while a majority of Indians still farm when 5-10 million would suffice.

ideas.idea: A tiny circle of competence is enough: John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford.
ideas.detail: Better to be an inch wide and a mile deep than a mile wide and an inch deep; understand very few businesses extremely well and invest when it appears you cannot lose.

ideas.idea: A commodity producer at the low end of the global cost curve with long reserves and no debt has a wide, deep moat and a license to print money.
ideas.detail: Saudi Aramco produced oil at $1-2 a barrel and would still profit at $20 when everyone else stopped; he owns a low-cost metallurgical coal producer close to port, with long-lived reserves and no debt, for which tariffs do not matter.

ideas.idea: He buys one or two things a year and would need no analysts; if the job is done right one never sells, and every sale means a mistake.
ideas.detail: He kept two helpers from a failed business for deep dives but does not let them generate ideas; the hunt is for no-brainer anomalies that hit you over the head with a two-by-four or a cricket bat.

ideas.idea: Invest when things make no sense: Turkey in 2018-19 screened extremely cheap with everyone exiting, with one company at a P/E of 0.1.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He visited companies in the portfolio of an Istanbul value-investor friend ('too much Graham, too little Munger'), doing no prior work and focusing on businesses immune to currency and inflation.

ideas.idea: Reysas was bought at a $16 million market cap against $800 million of liquidation value; six years later it is worth about a billion and liquidation value is $2-3 billion.
ideas.detail: Warehouses 99% leased to Amazon, Ikea, Carrefour, Mercedes, Toyota and DuPont on inflation-indexed or dollar/euro leases, worth $1 billion with $200 million debt; he got a third of the company for $8 million. Returns are infinite in lira and 16 million to a billion in dollars.

ideas.idea: Turkey's gambler culture, where the float cycles every 21 days, let him buy a third of Reysas; the market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive.
ideas.detail: Typical Turkish retail investors buy at 10 and sell at 3 for 10%; Buffett's quote could not be truer in Turkey.

ideas.idea: He treats Reysas as a family business with its founders and will not sell until they do, having discovered they are gifted capital allocators reinvesting at 20-35%-plus dollar returns.
ideas.detail: He meets them once a year over bluefish on the Bosphorus and has not seen a single mistake in six years; his main job is to do nothing and play bridge.

ideas.idea: His biggest flawed model was selling great businesses at 90% of intrinsic value to buy something half off, because intrinsic value is unknowable and great businesses are rare anomalies.
ideas.detail: Do not sell a great business when fully priced or even overpriced; sit until valuation becomes completely egregious. He hopes for 29 more years of compounding to apply the lesson.

ideas.idea: In 1995 he put $20,000 into Satyam, Kotak, Blue Dart and Sky Pack; Satyam went 140x by 2000 and he sold near the peak, then sold the others 'to clean up his books' and Kotak went 350x and Blue Dart 500x.
ideas.detail: Of $1 million starting capital, $10,000 in Satyam became $1.4 million and the US portfolio about $13 million; Falguni Nayar at Kotak's London office opened his account and impressed him into the last-minute Kotak bet. Exceptional management can do exceptional things you cannot put an intrinsic value on.

ideas.idea: Recognizing and hanging on to winners matters far more than avoiding value traps: a Nifty 50 portfolio with 98% going to zero but 2% in Walmart compounds at almost 15% for 55 years versus 10% for the S&P.
ideas.detail: The 1960s-70s Nifty 50 (ADP, McDonald's, Coke, P&G, Xerox, Polaroid, Kodak, Avon) was decimated in the 1973-74 crash. Templeton said the best are wrong one in three times, and only 12 of Buffett's 400-plus decisions in 60 years moved the needle for Berkshire, a 3-4% hit rate.
